```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
options(width = 90)
# The evaluated examples run against a local replay of responses recorded from
# the production API (tests/testthat/fixtures/recorded, tools/record_fixtures.R):
# the vignette builds without network and without a login, and the outputs
# shown are real outputs of the API.
soil <- soilhub:::replay_session()
```

This guide shows the first steps with **soilhub**, the R package of the
Global Soil Data Hub. With it you can see which soil datasets the hub holds
(WoSIS, WISE, SOTER, SOTWIS), how many profiles and measurements they have in
your area, and read the measurements into R as an ordinary data frame.

A few words used everywhere in the package (the help page `?soilhub-terms`
has the full list):

- a **feature** is a place: a soil profile site (a point) or a map unit (a
  polygon);
- a **profile** is the soil described at that place;
- a **horizon** is one layer of a profile, with an upper and a lower depth;
- an **observation** is one measured value (for example the organic carbon
  of one horizon).

**About the outputs shown here.** The results printed in this guide were
produced by the same functions on answers recorded from the Global Soil Data
Hub API (version 0.6.0) in October 2026. When you run the code yourself the
data come live from the hub, so some numbers may differ.

## 1. Install and load the package

The installation command is in the
[README](https://github.com/giulange/soilhub-r#readme) of the package. You
run it once. The package `sf` is optional: install it only if you want maps
and geometries.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("sf")   # optional, only for geometries
```

Every time you start R, load the package:

```{r}
library(soilhub)
```

## 2. Sign in

The hub needs to know who you are. You sign in with your university or hub
account through your web browser: R never sees your password.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
soil <- soil_connect()
```

What happens, step by step:

1. R prints a web address and a short code, like this:

   ```
   soilhub: to sign in, open https://kc.weatherprogapp.it/realms/ams/device and enter the code ABCD-EFGH
     The code is valid for 10m; waiting for the browser step...
   ```

2. Open the address in your browser (R may open it for you), type the code
   and sign in with your usual account.
3. Approve the request. Back in R, `soil_connect()` finishes by itself.

The object `soil` is your **session**: every function takes it as its first
argument. The session renews itself when needed, so you can keep working
for hours. If it expires (for example after a long pause), sign in again
with `soil_login(soil)`.

How long a session lasts is decided by the Keycloak server. Measured on
18 October 2026: the access token is valid for 2 hours and is renewed
automatically at your next call; a pause of 95 minutes without any call
did not end the session; a session lasts at most 9 hours from the sign-in,
then `soil_login(soil)` is needed.

## 3. What am I allowed to do?

Your account has **rights**. Most users have `soil:summary` (see what
exists) and `soil:read` (read the data). `soil_whoami()` shows your rights
and the functions they allow.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
soil_whoami(soil)
```

The output looks like this (shortened; the user name is yours):

```
#> <soil_identity> your-user-name
#>   Rights:  soil:summary, soil:read (audience soil-api)
#>   Token:   valid for 1h 59m (until ...)
#>   Session: renewable
#>   Functions by right:
#>     soil:summary  yes soil_capabilities(), soil_datasets(), ...
#>     soil:read     yes soil_observations(), soil_features(), ...
#>     soil:publish  no  soil_run_open(), soil_publish_values(), ...
#>     soil:admin    no  soil_register_variable(), soil_product(), ...
```

A "no" is normal for readers: publishing data is for a few accounts only.

## 4. Which datasets are there?

`soil_datasets()` returns one row per dataset of the hub.

```{r}
datasets <- soil_datasets(soil)
nrow(datasets)
```

The table has many columns (title, counts, licence, citation, release...).
Here we look at four of them:

```{r}
datasets[, c("name", "title", "profile_count", "horizon_count")]
```

The `name` column is the code you will use in the other functions (for
example `"wosis_points"`). `profile_count` and `horizon_count` tell you how
big each dataset is. The SOTER and SOTWIS **polygon** datasets are soil map
units: their horizons belong to the profiles that represent the map units.

To see everything about one dataset, use `soil_dataset()` with its name:

```{r}
soil_dataset(soil, "wosis_points")
```

This tells you where the data come from (the release), how much there is,
under which licence you may use it and how to cite it.

## 5. Which soil properties are measured?

`soil_variables()` lists the soil properties (the hub calls them
**variables**). Here we ask only for those of WoSIS:

```{r}
variables <- soil_variables(soil, dataset = "wosis_points")
nrow(variables)
```

```{r}
head(variables[, c("variable_code", "name")], 10)
```

The `variable_code` (for example `organic_carbon`) is the name of the column
you will find in your data. The `name` says what was measured, with the
method when it matters (pH in water or in CaCl2, bulk density dry or moist).

## 6. How much data is in my area?

Before reading data, ask how much there is. `soil_summary()` counts features,
horizons and observations of a selection without transferring them. Here:
WoSIS profiles in Kenya.

```{r}
kenya <- soil_summary(soil, datasets = "wosis_points", country = "KEN")
kenya
```

WoSIS has about 2,300 profiles in Kenya with some 46,000 measured values:
a size you can read directly. For very large selections (more than a million
observations) you would use an export instead (see
`vignette("exports", package = "soilhub")`).

## 7. Read the measurements

`soil_observations()` reads the data. You choose the dataset and the area.
Here the area is a box around Vancouver (Canada), given as
`c(west, south, east, north)` in degrees, and `max_rows = 5` keeps only the
first five rows for this example (leave it out to read everything).

```{r}
vancouver <- c(-123.3, 49.0, -122.9, 49.4)
x <- soil_observations(soil, datasets = "wosis_points", bbox = vancouver, max_rows = 5)
nrow(x)
```

The result is a data frame with **one row per horizon**. First the columns
that say where the horizon is:

```{r}
x[, c("feature_id", "horizon_name", "upper_depth_cm", "lower_depth_cm")]
```

Each `feature_id` is one profile site: here the first three rows are the
horizons F, Ae and Bf of one profile, from 0 to 17 cm. The first two lines
printed above the table (starting with `#`) are a short report of the
package: how many horizons and profiles were read, and the reminder that the
read is incomplete because we asked for 5 rows only.

Then the measurements. Each soil property has a group of columns: the value,
its unit, its method and `_n`.

```{r}
x[, c("horizon_name", "organic_carbon", "organic_carbon_units", "organic_carbon_n")]
```

`organic_carbon` is the measured value, `organic_carbon_units` its unit
(g/kg here), and `organic_carbon_n` how many measurements the source holds
for that horizon (1 here: one value per horizon).

A column is an ordinary R vector, so the usual functions work:

```{r}
x$ph_cacl2
mean(x$ph_cacl2)
```

`ph_cacl2` is the pH measured in a CaCl2 solution: these soils are very
acid (pH 3.5 to 4.2).

## 8. What does each column mean?

`soil_columns()` describes the measurement columns of your table: unit,
original code of the source, how many horizons have a value.

```{r}
info <- soil_columns(x)
info[, c("column", "units", "source_codes", "horizon_count", "multi_value_cells")]
```

`source_codes` is the original WoSIS code (`orgc` for organic carbon): the
package keeps the original terms of the source. `horizon_count` says how many
of the horizons read have a value: here bulk density was measured in one
horizon only.

**Cells with several values.** In WoSIS a few cells hold more than one
measurement of the same horizon (for example two clay contents from two
analyses). Then the column (for example `clay`) holds the **mean** of the
values, as WoSIS publishes it, and an extra column `clay_values` keeps all
the original values. `multi_value_cells` above counts such cells: there are
none in this small example, so there is no `_values` column.

## 9. Save your data

Save the table with `saveRDS()` and read it back later with `readRDS()`.
Here we use a temporary folder; use your own folder in practice.

```{r}
file <- file.path(tempdir(), "vancouver-horizons.rds")
saveRDS(x, file)
y <- readRDS(file)
nrow(y)
```

Save your **data**, never the session object `soil`: it contains your
sign-in, which must not end up in a file or in a shared project.

## 10. Cite the data

Every dataset has its own citation and licence. `soil_citations()` tells you
what to cite for the data you read:

```{r}
citations <- soil_citations(x)
citations$citation_text
```

`soil_licences(x)` gives the terms of use in the same way.

## 11. Sign out

At the end you can sign out; this forgets the sign-in kept in memory.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
soil_logout(soil)
```

## Where to go next

- `vignette("raw-vs-revised", package = "soilhub")`: the data as published by
  ISRIC, and the documented corrections you can ask for.
- `vignette("first-layer", package = "soilhub")`: the first (surface) layer
  of each profile, and the soil map components of SOTER and SOTWIS.
- `vignette("exports", package = "soilhub")`: large selections and files
  for GIS.
- `vignette("writing-data", package = "soilhub")`: publishing derived values
  (special rights needed).
- `vignette("migration-0.1", package = "soilhub")`: for users of the old
  0.1.x client.

```{r teardown, include = FALSE}
soilhub:::replay_stop(soil)
```
